Let  

\[
\{1,2,\dots ,2n\}=A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup\cdots\cup A_{n}
\qquad (|A_{i}|=2)
\]

and put \(s_i=\sum_{a\in A_i}a\).  
We have to find those \(n\in\mathbb N\) for which a partition can be chosen so that  

\[
P=\prod_{i=1}^{n}s_i
\]

is a perfect square.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Even \(n\)

Take the usual “mirror’’ pairing  

\[
(1,2n),\;(2,2n-1),\ldots,(n,n+1).
\]

Every pair has the same sum  

\[
s_i=1+2n=2n+1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
P=(2n+1)^{\,n}.
\]

If \(n\) is even, the exponent \(n\) is even; therefore every prime appears with an even exponent in \(P\) and \(P\) is a perfect square.  
Thus **every even \(n\) works.**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Odd \(n\)

First we exhibit a concrete example for the smallest odd case.

*For \(n=3\)*  

\[
(1,5),\;(2,4),\;(3,6)\qquad\Longrightarrow
\qquad s_1=s_2=6,\;s_3=9
\]

and  

\[
P=6\cdot6\cdot9=6^{2}\cdot9=(18)^{2},
\]

so \(n=3\) is admissible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Extending an odd solution

Assume we already have a suitable partition for an odd integer \(m\ge 3\).
From it we construct one for \(m+2\) (which is also odd).

The numbers \(1,\dots ,2m\) are already paired.  
Add the four new numbers  

\[
2m+1,\;2m+2,\;2m+3,\;2m+4 .
\]

Pair them as  

\[
(2m+1,\,2m+4),\qquad (2m+2,\,2m+3).
\]

Both new pairs have the same sum  

\[
(2m+1)+(2m+4)=(2m+2)+(2m+3)=4m+5 .
\]

Consequently the contribution of the two new pairs to the product is  

\[
(4m+5)^{2},
\]

a perfect square. Multiplying this by the already‑square product for the
first \(2m\) numbers we obtain a square product for the whole set
\(\{1,\dots ,2(m+2)\}\).  

Thus, by induction, **every odd integer \(n\ge 3\) admits a required
partition.**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The case \(n=1\)

For \(n=1\) the only possible pair is \((1,2)\) whose sum is \(3\); the
product \(3\) is not a square. Hence \(n=1\) does **not** work.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

All natural numbers except \(n=1\) possess a division of
\(\{1,2,\dots ,2n\}\) into \(n\) pairs whose sums give a square
product.

\[
\boxed{\;n\in\mathbb N,\;n\ge 2\;}
\]   (or “all natural numbers \(n>1\)”.)<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
